trace.title: HTTP and filters
trace.detail:
# The idea

An HTTP endpoint is a boundary. Treat incoming strings and JSON as untrusted input.

Binding turns JSON into Java values. Validation checks those values.

Authorization checks whether this caller may perform this action. These are separate steps.

Keep controller methods short. Convert input, call a use case, then map its result to an HTTP response.

Put reusable business rules in the service. Return DTOs, which are small request/response types, rather than exposing database entities and all their fields.

Choose errors that help the client: bad input is different from a missing record or a conflict. Do not return stack traces or SQL text to callers.

An exception handler can make the error shape consistent.

trace.title: Follow the middle steps
trace.detail:
A servlet filter can run before MVC. DispatcherServlet chooses a handler.

A message converter reads JSON. Validation runs on the bound input.

Then the controller invokes the service. The response converter writes JSON.

Try an empty title, malformed JSON, a valid request, and a simulated service conflict. For each, predict whether the service should run.

Use @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler for your domain errors. Log a request ID so an operator can find details privately.

trace.title: Check the result
trace.detail: Returning an entity can trigger lazy queries during JSON serialization or reveal an internal field. A 200 response containing {error: ...} also makes clients guess whether the operation succeeded.
